doc.title: Ellen Rowe interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 2, 2024

title: How advice to jazz students has changed since Connecticut
summary: Rowe compares advice at U Conn with now: jam sessions and working bands have faded, entrepreneurship and technology have opened new paths.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I’d like to start out with a question that’s been on my mind. If you think back to when you were at the University of Connecticut, earlier in your career, and you think of what you might have advised to jazz students back then and if you compare it with what you may do now, what are the significant differences?

That is an excellent question. Yeah, I think about that a good bit. I mean especially my faculty colleagues and I, if they’re over the age of 50 we find ourselves definitely questioning some things that we took for granted when we were first starting out to teach. And I’d say one of the big ones is that I think when I started at U Conn there’s still pretty much a tried and true way for young students to, you know, get their feet wet and go to the jam sessions that existed at the time, to point them towards working bands that still existed, and you know maybe even with the more famous ones saying look you know you’re not ready for this right now but these bands are out there and if you go to all these — you know if there’s somebody you want to play with and you go to all their gigs and you know just pester — not pester them in a bad way but you know let them know who you are and work on all their music and you know that used to be a big part of our spiel,

and I mean it still is in the sense that if somebody is in love with, you know, Brian Blade’s music and you know we’re certainly going to say hey go to all his gigs and try and get to know him and his players. But I think we are aware that students are learning, they are finding different paths and there’s so much entrepreneurship involved now because there’s so many different ways that students can get their music out there, can connect with other students, you know ways of creating their music that’s very different from before with, you know, all the DOSS and layering and you know the ease that they have with all kinds of technology. So I think what most of us have found is that we are trying to advise students down a lot of different paths. Like just you know saying there’s a lot of different avenues open to you now and still maintain every ounce of integrity, you know, that we can encourage them to have to be the very best players and composers they can be, to study the masters, but to just realize that there’s going to be different vehicles for them to get their music out there and to meet people and you know and of course there’s a lot more happening on line and things like that. That’s I’d say — and then also just that, you know even tunes that get played at jam sessions have evolved. I don’t mean evolved, I guess I should say changed. I don’t want to say the tunes they’re playing now are better or worse, but you know so there’s a different kind of, an expanding body of standard repertoire, let’s put it that way, that people need to know. So those are a few things. I’m sure I’ll think of some more but that’s part of it.
